prompt: List the name and salary of all Engineering employees, ordered by salary DESC. The Engineering department has `department_id = 1`.
constraints: Use department_id, not the text `department` column.
starter:
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE department_id = 1
ORDER BY ...;
hints: Filter with WHERE department_id = 1.
Order by salary DESC.
The text column `department` and the id column `department_id` both exist — prefer the id for joins/filters.

bruteForce.code: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE department = 'Engineering' ORDER BY salary DESC;
bruteForce.explanation: Works for this seed but couples to a text label — brittle if a department renames. Always prefer the FK id.

optimal.code:
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE department_id = 1
ORDER BY salary DESC;
optimal.explanation: Filter by FK, sort by salary descending. With an index on department_id this is an O(matches) seek.

prompt: List each employee's name alongside their department's name, ordered alphabetically by employee name. Exclude employees whose department is NULL.
constraints: Use an INNER JOIN — don't filter NULLs after the fact.
starter:
SELECT e.name, d.name AS dept_name
FROM employees e
...
ORDER BY e.name;
hints: INNER JOIN excludes rows where the ON match fails — which neatly excludes Frank's NULL department.
Both tables have a `name` column. Disambiguate with aliases or AS.
Order by employee name alphabetically.

bruteForce.code:
SELECT e.name, (SELECT d.name FROM departments d WHERE d.id = e.department_id) AS dept_name
FROM employees e
WHERE e.department_id IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY e.name;
bruteForce.explanation: Works but does a per-row subquery. Join is the idiomatic move.

optimal.code:
SELECT e.name, d.name AS dept_name
FROM employees e
INNER JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id
ORDER BY e.name;
optimal.explanation: INNER JOIN naturally drops rows where e.department_id is NULL (NULL never matches via =).

prompt: Find the names of employees who are not assigned to any department (department_id IS NULL).
constraints: One row in the seed: Frank.
hints: Equality against NULL never matches — use IS NULL.
Direct filter is simpler than LEFT JOIN here, but the LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL pattern is the general anti-join template.
`WHERE department_id = NULL` will return zero rows. Always use `IS NULL`.

bruteForce.code:
SELECT e.name
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id
WHERE d.id IS NULL;
bruteForce.explanation: The general anti-join: left join then keep only unmatched (NULL on the right) rows. Works even when the FK isn't already NULL.

optimal.explanation: Direct NULL filter — simplest when the column itself can be NULL. The bruteForce anti-join is the general technique when you want 'in A but not in B' across different tables.

prompt: For each department, output `dept_name` and `headcount` (number of employees). Include only departments with more than 1 employee. Order by headcount DESC, then dept_name ASC.
constraints: Use GROUP BY + HAVING. Skip Frank (NULL department).
starter:
SELECT d.name AS dept_name, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.id, d.name
HAVING ...
ORDER BY ...;
hints: INNER JOIN naturally excludes Frank (NULL department_id won't match).
GROUP BY the department, then COUNT(*) per group.
Filter groups with HAVING — not WHERE — because HAVING runs after grouping. Use `COUNT(*) > 1`.

bruteForce.code:
SELECT d.name, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees e WHERE e.department_id = d.id) AS headcount
FROM departments d
WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees e WHERE e.department_id = d.id) > 1
ORDER BY headcount DESC, d.name;
bruteForce.complexity: O(d * n) — correlated subquery twice per department
bruteForce.explanation: Functional but does the same count twice. GROUP BY + HAVING is the standard one-pass solution.

optimal.code:
SELECT d.name AS dept_name, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.id, d.name
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY headcount DESC, dept_name ASC;
optimal.explanation: Group, count, filter. HAVING is for post-aggregation filtering (you can't put COUNT(*) > 1 in WHERE because aggregates don't exist yet at WHERE-time).

prompt: For each department, output `dept_name` and `avg_salary` (integer-cast average), ordered alphabetically by dept_name. Skip employees with NULL department.
constraints: Use CAST(AVG(salary) AS INTEGER) to dodge floating-point representation issues.
starter:
SELECT d.name AS dept_name, CAST(AVG(e.salary) AS INTEGER) AS avg_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
hints: Average of integers in SQLite returns a REAL. CAST to INTEGER (truncates) for predictable output.
GROUP BY the department.
INNER JOIN excludes Frank (NULL department) — AVG would skip his NULL anyway, but the join also drops the row entirely.

bruteForce.code:
SELECT (SELECT name FROM departments WHERE id = e.department_id) AS dept_name,
       CAST(AVG(salary) AS INTEGER) AS avg_salary
FROM employees e
WHERE department_id IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY department_id
ORDER BY dept_name;
bruteForce.complexity: Works but does a per-row name lookup
bruteForce.explanation: Functional. A direct JOIN is cleaner.

optimal.code:
SELECT d.name AS dept_name, CAST(AVG(e.salary) AS INTEGER) AS avg_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.id, d.name
ORDER BY d.name;
optimal.explanation: JOIN + GROUP BY. CAST forces integer truncation so the test result is deterministic.

prompt: Find employees whose salary is STRICTLY greater than the average salary of their own department. Output `name`, `salary`. Order by name ASC. Skip employees with NULL department.
constraints: Use a correlated subquery (or a window function) for the per-dept average.
starter:
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees e
WHERE department_id IS NOT NULL
  AND salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees e2 WHERE e2.department_id = e.department_id)
ORDER BY name;
hints: Correlated subquery: for each employee e, compute AVG over employees in e's department.
Compare with > (strictly greater), so an employee earning exactly the average is excluded.
Window function alternative: AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department_id) inside a CTE, then filter.

bruteForce.code:
SELECT e.name, e.salary
FROM employees e
WHERE e.department_id IS NOT NULL
  AND e.salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees e2 WHERE e2.department_id = e.department_id)
ORDER BY e.name;
bruteForce.explanation: Logically clean. Modern planners often rewrite this as a join + window function, but pessimistically it's quadratic.

optimal.code:
WITH dept_avg AS (
  SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal FROM employees
  WHERE department_id IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY department_id
)
SELECT e.name, e.salary
FROM employees e
JOIN dept_avg da ON e.department_id = da.department_id
WHERE e.salary > da.avg_sal
ORDER BY e.name;
optimal.explanation: Pre-aggregate once, then a single join. Window-function form (AVG ... OVER (PARTITION BY department_id)) is also clean.

prompt: Bucket employees into salary tiers and count each tier. Tiers: `low` (salary < 40000), `mid` (40000 ≤ salary ≤ 70000), `high` (salary > 70000). Output `tier`, `n` ordered tier-alphabetically. Include all employees including Frank.
constraints: Use CASE WHEN inside a CTE.

examples.output: high 2 (Alice, Carol), low 2 (Eve, Frank), mid 4 (Bob, Dave, Grace, Hugo)

starter:
WITH tiered AS (
  SELECT name,
         CASE WHEN salary < 40000 THEN 'low'
              WHEN salary <= 70000 THEN 'mid'
              ELSE 'high'
         END AS tier
  FROM employees
)
SELECT tier, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM tiered
GROUP BY tier
ORDER BY tier;
hints: CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END returns a value per row — that becomes the bucket label.
Wrap the CASE in a CTE, then GROUP BY the alias.
Order: CASE conditions are evaluated top-to-bottom; first match wins. Put the most specific first.

bruteForce.code:
SELECT 'low' AS tier, COUNT(*) AS n FROM employees WHERE salary < 40000
UNION ALL
SELECT 'mid', COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE salary >= 40000 AND salary <= 70000
UNION ALL
SELECT 'high', COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE salary > 70000
ORDER BY tier;
bruteForce.explanation: Works but scans three times. The CTE+CASE approach scans once.

optimal.code:
WITH tiered AS (
  SELECT CASE WHEN salary < 40000 THEN 'low'
              WHEN salary <= 70000 THEN 'mid'
              ELSE 'high'
         END AS tier
  FROM employees
)
SELECT tier, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM tiered
GROUP BY tier
ORDER BY tier;
optimal.explanation: CASE assigns a tier in one scan; GROUP BY tier aggregates. CTE is for readability — could inline the CASE in the GROUP BY column too.

prompt: For each customer who has placed at least one DELIVERED order, output `customer_name` and `total_spend` (sum over order_items of qty × price). Order by total_spend DESC. Exclude cancelled and shipped orders.
constraints: Three-table join: customers + orders + order_items + products.
starter:
SELECT c.name AS customer_name, SUM(oi.quantity * p.price) AS total_spend
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY total_spend DESC;
hints: You need price (from products) and quantity (from order_items) per line item — that's a 4-table join.
Filter status = 'delivered' BEFORE aggregating.
GROUP BY customer; SUM(qty * price) per group.

bruteForce.code:
SELECT c.name,
  (SELECT SUM(oi.quantity * p.price)
   FROM orders o
   JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
   JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.id
   WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'delivered'
  ) AS total_spend
FROM customers c
WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'delivered') > 0
ORDER BY total_spend DESC;
bruteForce.explanation: Works but does multiple correlated subqueries. The join + group-by version is cleaner and faster.

optimal.code:
SELECT c.name AS customer_name, SUM(oi.quantity * p.price) AS total_spend
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY total_spend DESC;
optimal.explanation: Single grouped query; the join produces one row per line-item then SUM collapses to one per customer. Inner joins naturally exclude customers with no delivered orders.

prompt: List products that have never appeared in a DELIVERED order. Output `name` (alphabetical).
constraints: Use NOT EXISTS (handles NULLs safely; NOT IN can trip on NULL subqueries).

examples.input: ecommerce: deliveries cover Laptop, Phone, Headphones

starter:
SELECT name
FROM products p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.id
  WHERE oi.product_id = p.id AND o.status = 'delivered'
)
ORDER BY name;
hints: Anti-join pattern: 'products NOT in (products with a delivered order)'.
NOT EXISTS is safer than NOT IN because of NULL semantics; here either works since product_id is NOT NULL.
Inside NOT EXISTS, SELECT 1 is idiomatic — we don't care about the columns, just whether a row exists.

bruteForce.code:
SELECT name
FROM products
WHERE id NOT IN (
  SELECT DISTINCT oi.product_id
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.id
  WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
)
ORDER BY name;
bruteForce.complexity: Works but fragile if product_id could be NULL
bruteForce.explanation: NOT IN works here because product_id is NOT NULL. In schemas where it could be NULL, NOT IN would silently return zero rows.

optimal.code:
SELECT name
FROM products p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.id
  WHERE oi.product_id = p.id AND o.status = 'delivered'
)
ORDER BY name;
optimal.explanation: Correlated NOT EXISTS — for each product, check if any delivered-order line item references it. Robust to NULLs. Engines optimize this to an anti-semi-join.

prompt: Find the top 3 highest-paid employees. Output `name` and `salary`, ordered by salary DESC.
starter:
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 3;
hints: ORDER BY salary DESC, then LIMIT 3.
For top-K per group (e.g. top 3 per department), use ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department).
Beware ties: LIMIT 3 picks any 3 if a tie spans the boundary. DENSE_RANK() handles tie-aware top-K.

bruteForce.explanation: Roundabout. Direct ORDER BY + LIMIT is the standard pattern.

optimal.code: SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 3;
optimal.complexity: O(n) scan + sort, or O(n log k) with a heap if the engine optimizes
optimal.explanation: Standard top-K pattern. Engines may use a heap of size K instead of full sort.

prompt: Assign a rank to each employee within their department based on their salary in descending order. Return the department name as `dept_name`, employee name as `employee_name`, `salary`, and the rank as `salary_rank`. Exclude employees with no department. Order by `dept_name` ASC, `salary_rank` ASC.
constraints: Use RANK() or DENSE_RANK() as a window function.
starter:
SELECT d.name AS dept_name, e.name AS employee_name, e.salary,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...) AS salary_rank
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id
ORDER BY dept_name, salary_rank;
hints: Join employees to departments to get `dept_name`.
Partition by `d.id` or `d.name` and order by `salary DESC` inside the window function.
Order the final output by `dept_name` ASC and `salary_rank` ASC.

bruteForce.code:
SELECT d.name AS dept_name, e.name AS employee_name, e.salary,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees e2 WHERE e2.department_id = e.department_id AND e2.salary >= e.salary) AS salary_rank
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id
ORDER BY dept_name, salary_rank;
bruteForce.explanation: Correlated count of employees with higher salary. Easy to write but slow.

optimal.code:
SELECT d.name AS dept_name, e.name AS employee_name, e.salary,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY d.id ORDER BY e.salary DESC) AS salary_rank
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id
ORDER BY dept_name, salary_rank;
optimal.explanation: DENSE_RANK() OVER partition ranks employees by salary descending within department. The join retrieves department names.
